messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
parts:
I think one way to take the burden off the interfaces
checking consistency of commands is to break the monolithic
command-line call down into multiple little function calls.
In that situation, almost everything will be consistent.

R goes partway down this path, but not all the way, because
the stan() function still encompasses both NUTS and HMC.

For example, if the commands were

* stan_sample_nuts(...)
* stan_sample_hmc(...)
* stan_optimize_lbfgs(...)
* stan_optimize_bfgs(...)

(The names aren't important, so please don't get hung up here if
you think they should say "bayes" or "mcmc" or "(p)mle" or "map"
or "mode" or whatever.)

Then almost all of the built-in options will be legal. To work
this out in more detail for nuts, here are all the config options
(including model, which is implicit in CmdStan):

nuts(model (file | string | dynamic-object),
max_depth (int > 0),
metric (unit | diag |dense),
stepsize (double > 0),
stepsize_jitter (double in (0,1)),
num_samples (int >= 0),
num_warmup (int >= 0),
save_warmup (bool),
thin (int >= 1),
adapt(false | true
| dictionary(gamma (double in ?),
delta (double in (0,1)),
kappa (double in ?),
t0 (double in ?)),
data (var_dictionary),
init (double > 0 | var_dictionary),
seed (int in (0,2^32 - 1)),
output_file (file),
diagnostic_file (file),
refresh (int >= 0) );

That's it. Now if within Python or R, you have some simple
routines to validate ranges and validate the various values, you'd
be good to go without any complicated config construction or
callbacks. These routines could be used across the different
functions.

This doesn't specify defaults, but presumably that's also easy.

Adaptation is worth special attention, because it's
a big disjunction that's either boolean with defaults or
specifies overrides in terms of a nested argument.

The huge advantage is that the error messages will match what
the names are in RStan or PyStan.

I'm not sure if allowing the disjunctive types, like init
is a good idea in R or Python. If you have two different
arguments, then there are consistency requirements, so I'd
rather see that as a substructure, just as in CmdStan.

Then, to run, there needs to be a way to turn these
into a config C++ object that can actually be passed to
the Stan C++ to do the work, but that shouldn't be that
hard, either.

I'd like to compare how much work this would be to
marshaling a config object from a similar input in a dictionary,
converting to JSON, sending it to Stan C++ for validation,
then interpreting the results back in terms of the actual
argument names in PyStan or RStan.

This seems way more modular to me and doesn't require
any kind of config within Stan C++ --- it all becomes
a C++ structure that just runs and then CmdStan would get
all the config stuff that's currently in Stan C++.

- Bob

parts:
Surprise! I fundamentally disagree.

The problem with splitting up the API into a bunch of small functions
is that we have no way to enforcing a consistent user experience
which will force users to learn each interface separately. We’re
already seeing this in RStan which is rapidly drifting from CmdStan
(and hence JuliaStan and MatlabStan) and taking PyStan with it.
It’s already a pain in the ass to do these workshops where I have to
relearn all of the idiosyncrasies of each interface in addition to all
of the usual work.

Then there’s the problem of actually implementing an interface,
which would now require the implementer to come up with a user
experience and piece together all of the modular components.

I am very much in favor of having a monolithic API route that
provides at least a marginal enforcement of a unified user
experience. Interfaces will always be able to screw it up with
enough work but the path of least resistance will be a similar
user experience everywhere.

> The problem with splitting up the API into a bunch of small functions

This is the key to the disagreement, and I disagree very
strongly.

I think the experience from R should be R-like, from
Python should be Pythonic (can't believe I just said that),

the R user experience look like this:

> foo("sample algorithm=hmc metric=unit_e engine=nuts max_depth=15 data file=model.data.R init=modelinit.R random seed=5 output file=samples.csv");

no way of passing inits in as a function, no way of passing data
in as list, no plotting, etc. Basically nothing's that not
built into CmdStan.

without straying too far from the command line you set up:

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
parts:
I think there's a great deal everyone agrees on. Splitting up the
interface into smaller functions sounds good to me, but perhaps that can
be tabled until Stan 3.0 and the proposed reorganization of
RStan/PyStan.

As for the general question of how to provide parameters, I think
there's probably some middle ground we can reach. Those using Stan know
they are getting into a DSL, so we have *some* freedom to depart from
Pythonic and R styles. We already all agree, for example, that the
parameters should have the same names (i.e., "adapt_t0" and not
"adapt.t0"). I think we can make other small concessions here in order
to have an experience that is as consistent as possible. I want
switching between R and Python to be as painless as possible.)

I think there are two important things that the Stan C++ services
library should provide:

- Validation of config (e.g., is adapt_int_buffer positive)
- One source of truth about default values.

While promoting code reuse is the proximate goal, just having
RStan/PyStan and CmdStan on the same page about something as modest as
config validation would probably do more in the short term to move us
towards a consistent user experience than anything else I can think of.

Best,

Allen

This sounds good to me (serializing/deserializing a C++ object). I'd
still like to consider Protocol Buffers here instead of JSON here
because PB is/are fast (I think we could even put initial values and
data in there) and there's the explicit schema that everyone can read
(which JSON would lack). Moreover, you can specify some consistency
requirements in Protocol Buffers explicitly (see Union Types,
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/techniques#union).
Clearly Python and R will need to know something about what a valid
config looks like -- but I'd prefer that they need not have to know too
much.

As for passing large amounts of data via Protocol Buffers, there's this
magical-sounding "ZeroCopy" functionality provided by PB that sounds
pretty good
(https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.io.zero_copy_stream#ZeroCopyInputStream).

Best,

-a

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
parts:
Let me be more particular about what I mean:

The C++ code needs a few things from each interface
in order to be executed — a configuration, from where
certain info will be obtained (data, initialization, etc), 
and from where certain info will be written (info, errors,
output, diagnostics, etc).  

The interfaces can implement these however they want,
so for example CmdStan can grab inputs from files
where as RStan and PyStan can grab them from the
local environment (making the experience appropriate
to their respective environments).  Same with the outputs.
The implementations vary but the basic interaction is
the same.

Where our disagreements lie is with the configuration.
Firstly, I want every interface to run the same optimization,
sampling, and diagnostic routines so that a user can
switch interfaces and have the same functionality —
I don’t see how this is guaranteed without enforcing
a monolithic function.  

Secondly, I want _every_  configuration option available
from each interface so it’s just as easy to, say, tweak the 
step size in RStan as it is in CmdStan (the “control” 
interface makes me sad every time I have to get in there).
Again, how the configuration is constructed can vary
by interface (string, nested dict, list, etc) but I feel
strongly that the configuration itself is uniform.

If we just give the interfaces a mess of routes and let
them do what they want I don’t see how we can guarantee
any uniformity of experience across the interfaces.

On Mar 18, 2015, at 10:40 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:


On Mar 18, 2015, at 8:45 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Surprise!  I fundamentally disagree.

Surprise, surprise, no surprise (Dr. Seuss-isms just
for Andrew).

The problem with splitting up the API into a bunch of small functions
is that we have no way to enforcing a consistent user experience

This is the key to the disagreement, and I disagree very
strongly.

I think the experience from R should be R-like, from
Python should be Pythonic (can't believe I just said that),
and from the command line, should be shellish.

The only way to make everything literally the same would be to have
the R user experience look like this:

stan_make("foo.stan");

foo("sample algorithm=hmc metric=unit_e engine=nuts max_depth=15 data file=model.data.R init=modelinit.R random seed=5 output file=samples.csv");

stan_print("samples.csv")

No way of doing extract, no way of calling log prob directly,
no way of passing inits in as a function, no way of passing data
in as list, no plotting, etc.  Basically nothing's that not 
built into CmdStan.

I guess we could use list notation to make it a bit more R-like,
without straying too far from the command line you set up:

foo(list("sample", algorithm=list("hmc",metric="unit_e", engine=list("nuts", max_depth=15), data=list(file="model.data.R"), init="model.init.R",random=list(seed="5")...);

Is this what you are envisioning?  If not, would you mind elaborating
a bit on what you think the R user experience should be? 

which will force users to learn each interface separately.

I don't think many users are going to learn multiple Stan
interfaces, so I think that's a moot point other than for us,
as you note in the next paragraph.

We’re
already seeing this in RStan which is rapidly drifting from CmdStan
(and hence JuliaStan and MatlabStan) and taking PyStan with it.
It’s already a pain in the ass to do these workshops where I have to
relearn all of the idiosyncrasies of each interface in addition to all
of the usual work.  

I feel your pain there.  Why not just do the workshops using
CmdStan only?  I'm doing one next week exclusively in RStan.
Then I believe Andrew, Daniel, and I will be doing a three-day
course using just RStan.

Then there’s the problem of actually implementing an interface,

This is a separate issue.  

To clarify, I'm *not* still advocating a modular approach on
the R side where we expose samplers, etc.  You and Daniel
convinced me that would be too hard to maintain.

What I'm suggesting is having the interface provide an idiomatic
way of piecing together a C++ structure (including
writers, iostreams, etc.) that would be passed to Stan C++
and further validated on that side to make sure nothing untoward
happens. 

Then no holds barred once the data gets back on the interface
side.  

You'll never be able to agree with Andrew as to what the
default print should look like.  You'll be stuck on scientific
notation before even getting going.

which would now require the implementer to come up with a user
experience and piece together all of the modular components.

Back to the first disagreement.  I think that's a good thing!  
Otherwise, we wind up with every interface looking like the
command line and being heavily limited in what it offers.

I am very much in favor of having a monolithic API route that
provides at least a marginal enforcement of a unified user
experience.  Interfaces will always be able to screw it up with
enough work but the path of least resistance will be a similar
user experience everywhere.

Could you please sketch out what you think the R user experience
would look like so as to match the one in CmdStan?  Or Python's?

- Bob


On Mar 18, 2015, at 4:39 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

I think one way to take the burden off the interfaces 
checking consistency of commands is to break the monolithic
command-line call down into multiple little function calls.
In that situation, almost everything will be consistent.

R goes partway down this path, but not all the way, because
the stan() function still encompasses both NUTS and HMC.

For example, if the commands were

* stan_sample_nuts(...)
* stan_sample_hmc(...)
* stan_optimize_lbfgs(...)
* stan_optimize_bfgs(...)

(The names aren't important, so please don't get hung up here if
you think they should say "bayes" or "mcmc" or "(p)mle" or "map" 
or "mode" or whatever.)

Then almost all of the built-in options will be legal.  To work
this out in more detail for nuts, here are all the config options
(including model, which is implicit in CmdStan):

nuts(model (file | string | dynamic-object),
  max_depth (int > 0),
  metric (unit | diag |dense),
  stepsize (double > 0),
  stepsize_jitter (double in (0,1)),
  num_samples (int >= 0),
  num_warmup (int >= 0),
  save_warmup (bool),
  thin (int >= 1),
  adapt(false | true
        | dictionary(gamma (double in ?),
                    delta (double in (0,1)),
                    kappa (double in ?),
                    t0 (double in ?)),
  data (var_dictionary),
  init (double > 0 | var_dictionary),
  seed (int in (0,2^32 - 1)),
  output_file (file),
  diagnostic_file (file),
  refresh (int >= 0) );

That's it.  Now if within Python or R, you have some simple
routines to validate ranges and validate the various values, you'd
be good to go without any complicated config construction or
callbacks.  These routines could be used across the different
functions. 

This doesn't specify defaults, but presumably that's also easy.

Adaptation is worth special attention, because it's
a big disjunction that's either boolean with defaults or
specifies overrides in terms of a nested argument.

The huge advantage is that the error messages will match what
the names are in RStan or PyStan.  

I'm not sure if allowing the disjunctive types, like init
is a good idea in R or Python.  If you have two different
arguments, then there are consistency requirements, so I'd
rather see that as a substructure, just as in CmdStan.

Then, to run, there needs to be a way to turn these
into a config C++ object that can actually be passed to
the Stan C++ to do the work, but that shouldn't be that
hard, either.  

I'd like to compare how much work this would be to
marshaling a config object from a similar input in a dictionary,
converting to JSON, sending it to Stan C++ for validation,
then interpreting the results back in terms of the actual
argument names in PyStan or RStan.

This seems way more modular to me and doesn't require
any kind of config within Stan C++ --- it all becomes
a C++ structure that just runs and then CmdStan would get
all the config stuff that's currently in Stan C++.

- Bob

Wouldn’t the second and third steps be wrapped together?
As in you construct a config object, pass it into the Stan
call, and then get back your results.

> Do you object to all the additional functions inside R,
> like extract() and what not? Or do you object to the
> what Ben's calling "andrewfy", which was formerly referred

> in the previous message. Is the lack of a counter-proposal
> implicit acknowledgment that what I wrote is what you'd like
> to see in RStan?

If we wanted to be _really_ consistent amongst the interfaces
then the UX would be something like

1) Preprocessing
2) Compile Stan object/executable
3) Configure algorithm arguments and callbacks
4) Call Stan object/executable with configuration, returning results in fit object
5) Postprocessing

(1) and (5) are left to the interfaces so we don’t have to worry about those.
Each interface can add whatever functionality it wants here, such as print
and fit, although it would be great to unity these as much as possible.

(2) and (4) is a bit tricky because right now RStan and PyStan try to wrap
these together which necessitates tricks like Sebastian’s function. Personally
I’d much rather have the user create an explicit object and then call a run method
of that object, so if you want to rerun without recompiling you just call the
method again instead of creating a new object (this also parallels the CmdStan
procedure).

(4) is also completed in RStan and PyStan because the results aren’t
uniformly accessible. Instead you have to access the samples
and the sampler parameters separately in incredibly annoying ways,
but this is just a disagreement about exactly what extract should return.

My big complaint is in (3) which is where some of the biggest disparities
are (i.e. that awkward control list). The config can be implemented by
each interface separately but the user should have access to the
arguments in roughly the same way — for example, if we maintain the
current hierarchical structure then there should be some way of
specifying the config hierarchically. The flattened single arguments of
RStan and PyStan upsets me.
> What kind of drift are you talking about specifically?

In terms of time-dependence I’m specifically referring to all of these
functions that try to wrap RStan functionality into a UX that’s moving
further and further away from how the other interfaces are implemented.

(2) and (4) is a bit tricky because right now RStan and PyStan try to wrap

I’d much rather have the user create an explicit object and then call a run method

The stan() function does (2), (3), and (4) together but it is possible to do them separately. Or technically, you can do (2) separately but (3) and (4) are lumped together. In any event, if necessary, we could change that. We could even use more Pythonic calling semantics

model <- stan_model("foo.stan")
model$config(adapt_delta = 0.9)
model$sampling()
model$summary()

The only difficulty is that such idioms are relatively new to the R language and people (especially Andrew) are not used to them. It isn't a technical problem. I do mostly agree with Bob that the interfaces should behave more like the external software, although in this case it would be more a case of RStan behaving more like R will a few years in the future.

My big complaint is in (3) which is where some of the biggest disparities
are (i.e. that awkward control list).  The config can be implemented by
each interface separately but the user should have access to the
arguments in roughly the same way — for example, if we maintain the
current hierarchical structure then there should be some way of
specifying the config hierarchically.  The flattened single arguments of
RStan and PyStan upsets me.

That is not inherent either. Lots of R functions take a flat control list but we could specify that in a hierarchical fashion with either a list of lists or a JSON thing. Almost no one would even notice if we changed it completely.

RStan could adapt to almost anything and I think PyStan could as well. We just need to come to an agreement on monolithic config vs. modular and JSON vs. Protocol Buffers and things like that.

Ben

procedure).

The stan() function does (2), (3), and (4) together but it is possible to do them separately. Or technically, you can do (2) separately but (3) and (4) are lumped together. In any event, if necessary, we could change that. We could even use more Pythonic calling semantics

model <- stan_model("foo.stan")
model$config(adapt_delta = 0.9)
model$sampling()
model$summary()

The only difficulty is that such idioms are relatively new to the R language and people (especially Andrew) are not used to them. It isn't a technical problem. I do mostly agree with Bob that the interfaces should behave more like the external software, although in this case it would be more a case of RStan behaving more like R will a few years in the future.
 
My big complaint is in (3) which is where some of the biggest disparities
are (i.e. that awkward control list).  The config can be implemented by
each interface separately but the user should have access to the
arguments in roughly the same way — for example, if we maintain the
current hierarchical structure then there should be some way of
specifying the config hierarchically.  The flattened single arguments of
RStan and PyStan upsets me.

That is not inherent either. Lots of R functions take a flat control list but we could specify that in a hierarchical fashion with either a list of lists or a JSON thing. Almost no one would even notice if we changed it completely.

RStan could adapt to almost anything and I think PyStan could as well. We just need to come to an agreement on monolithic config vs. modular and JSON vs. Protocol Buffers and things like that.

Ben
